title: Krishna Consoles the Gopis
story:
When the sun rose over Vrindavan, the gopis were still weeping.

They were the cowherd women of the village, and Krishna — the boy who had grown up among them — was going away to Mathura that morning. The king of the city had sent for him, and nothing they could do would keep him. Through the dark hours they had sat where his voice had last reached them, calling his name into the night, and the night had given back only the sound of their own crying.

Now the morning was here — the sun climbing over the trees of Vrindavan, the first light falling on the road to Mathura — and the thing they had dreaded began to happen.

Nanda and the cowherds set out behind the chariot with their carts, and the whole village stirred into motion toward the city. The gopis went too. They could not stay behind, and they could not bear to let him go, so they walked on foot after the chariot that carried Krishna. And something strange came over them as they walked: just to follow him a little longer, to keep the shape of him in their eyes, softened their grief into something almost like gladness. Their tears had not quite stopped, but the road itself had become a kind of comfort — each step was a step beside him, and while he was still ahead of them, he was not yet gone.

From the chariot, Krishna saw them. He saw how his leaving had undone them — how they had poured themselves out along the road behind him, weeping and refusing to turn home. And he would not go without a word. He sent messengers back to them with a promise he asked them to keep. He would come back. I will return to you.

The words reached them along the road, his own voice carried back to them, and they were not a comfort offered from a distance — they were something he was asking of them. He had not forgotten them; he was trusting them with a promise. They were to carry it home and keep it there, like a lamp kept burning in an empty house against the family's return.

So they followed for as long as they could — while the banner of his chariot was still to be seen above the road, while the dust of its wheels still hung in the air behind him. They fixed their eyes on that banner and that dust, as though keeping them in sight could keep him there. The road stretched away toward Mathura, and the whole company of the village — the carts, the cowherds, the women on foot — moved along it the way a river moves.

But at last the banner sank out of view, and the last of the dust settled back to earth, and Krishna did not turn back. Then hope went out of them, and they turned homeward. And as they walked, they sang of him — of the deeds he had done, the days they had shared — keeping his name alive on the empty road until he should make good his word. The road that had carried him away from them carried their voices back the other way, and the singing did what weeping could not: it turned their faces homeward while their hearts stayed with him.
reflection: The consolation here is not a speech but a promise, sent back along the road the gopis are refusing to leave. It is the smallest thing in the story, and the largest: one sentence, carried by messengers, that gives them the strength to turn around.
next_story_tease: But at the river Yamuna, Akrura would stop to bathe — and in its waters he would see something he never imagined.
hero_scene: The gopis walking after Krishna's departing chariot on the road out of Vrindavan, their eyes fixed on the chariot's banner and the dust of its wheels, as the sun rises behind them.
